questions.q: A version control system (VCS) is best described as a tool that:
options: records the changes made to a set of files over time, so that any earlier version can be recovered
compresses a project folder into a single archive so that it takes up less disk space
checks a program for syntax errors before it is allowed to run
translates source code into an executable program
questions.explain: Version control exists to keep a history. Every change is recorded along with who made it and when, so you can inspect, compare with, or return to any earlier state of the project. Compression, error checking and translation belong to entirely different kinds of tools.
why_wrong: That describes an archiving or zip tool; a VCS stores history, and saving disk space is not its purpose.
Checking code for syntax errors is the job of a compiler or an editor's checker, not of version control.
Turning source code into a runnable program is done by a compiler; a VCS never compiles anything.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT something a version control system gives you?
options: a record of who changed what, and when
the ability to return the project to an earlier working state
branches, so an idea can be tried without disturbing the working version
a guarantee that the code you commit contains no bugs
questions.explain: Version control manages history, not quality. It will store a broken version just as faithfully as a working one; what it gives you is the ability to see exactly what changed and to go back if the change was a mistake. Finding bugs is the job of testing and review.
why_wrong: This is one of the main reasons version control exists: every recorded change carries an author and a date.
Reverting to an earlier version is a genuine benefit; the history is kept precisely so you can go back.
Branching is a real feature of version control, letting you experiment apart from the main line of work.

questions.q: Priya's folder contains project.doc, project_final.doc, project_final2.doc and project_FINAL_really.doc, and she can no longer tell which one her teammate edited last. Which choice solves the problem at its root?
options: Rename every copy with the date and time it was saved, so that the newest one is obvious
Put the project under version control, keeping one set of files with a recorded history of every change
Zip the whole folder at the end of each day and keep the zip files as backups
Email the newest copy to herself and her teammate after every editing session
questions.explain: The pile of files called final is exactly the problem version control was invented to end. Under a VCS there is one current set of files, and every earlier state lives in the recorded history together with its author, date and message, so which is newest and who changed this stop being guesswork.
why_wrong: Dated names are still manual copies: nothing records what changed or who changed it, and the folder only keeps growing.
Daily zips are backups, not history: they cannot tell her what changed or who edited it, and the copies still multiply.
Emailing copies multiplies the versions further, and gives two people editing at the same time no way to combine their work.

questions.q: In a local version control system the versions of a project are kept in a database on a single computer. What is its main drawback?
options: It can store only one earlier version of each file
Nobody else can collaborate on the project, and if that computer fails the whole history goes with it
A network connection is needed before any version can be saved
Every collaborator is forced to keep a complete copy of the history
questions.explain: A local VCS keeps its database on one machine only. That machine is a single point of failure, and there is no shared copy for teammates to work from. Those two limits are exactly why centralized and then distributed systems were developed.
why_wrong: A local VCS keeps many versions; storing a full history is its entire purpose.
Needing to reach a server is a limitation of centralized systems; a local system works entirely offline.
Full copies of the history on every machine describe a distributed system such as Git, not a local one.

questions.q: Which pair are both examples of centralized version control systems?
options: Git and Mercurial
Subversion (SVN) and CVS
GitHub and GitLab
RCS and Git
questions.explain: A centralized system keeps one repository, holding all the history, on a server; developers check out a working copy from it. Subversion and CVS are the standard examples. Git and Mercurial are distributed, while GitHub and GitLab are websites that host Git repositories rather than version control systems in their own right.
why_wrong: Both of these are distributed systems, in which each developer clones the full repository and its history.
These are hosting platforms for Git repositories, not version control systems themselves.
RCS is a local system and Git is distributed, so neither one is centralized.

questions.q: A small company keeps all its code in one Subversion repository on a single office server, and no backups are taken. The server's disk fails completely. What is the most serious consequence?
options: The entire project history is at risk, because it existed only on that server
Nothing is lost, because a centralized system automatically stores the history on every developer's machine
Only the changes each developer made since their last commit are lost
Only the newest version is lost, since older versions are always kept on the developers' computers
questions.explain: In a centralized system the server holds the single repository and the complete history, while developers hold only a checked-out snapshot of the current files. Lose the server with no backup and the history goes with it. This single point of failure is one of the reasons distributed systems, where every clone is itself a full copy, became popular.
why_wrong: Holding the history on every machine is a property of distributed systems; in a centralized system it lives on the server only.
Losing only uncommitted work would be true if every developer held a full copy of the history, which is the distributed model.
Developers hold only a working copy of the current files, so the older versions are not sitting on their machines.

questions.q: Ananya edits three files, runs git add . and stops for the day. The next morning git log shows no new entry for that work. What is the explanation?
options: git add only moved the changes into the staging area; nothing enters the repository's history until she runs git commit
git log lists only the commits made by other people, so her own work never appears in it
git add holds changes only while the terminal window stays open, so closing it discarded them
The work was committed, but git log needs an internet connection before it can display commits
questions.explain: Git moves a change through three areas: the working directory where you edit, the staging area that git add marks as ready, and the repository where git commit stores it permanently. Ananya stopped after staging, so the history has nothing new to show. Running git commit with a message is what creates the entry that git log then reports.
why_wrong: git log shows every commit in the repository, the author's own included, listed newest first.
Staged changes are recorded inside the .git folder on disk, so they survive closing the terminal or restarting the machine.
git log reads the local repository, which is why it works perfectly offline, and in any case nothing had been committed yet.

questions.q: Arjun is on a long train journey with no internet, yet he still makes several commits and reads through the project's history on his laptop. Why does this work?
options: Git is distributed, so his clone holds the full repository and history, and committing and reading the log are local operations
GitHub keeps a copy of the repository that his laptop can read without any connection
Git is centralized, so it only needs to contact the server about once a day
Git stores the commands and actually carries them out later, when the network returns
questions.explain: When you clone with Git you receive the entire repository, history included, onto your own machine. Commits are written straight into that local repository, so no server is involved and the operations are fast. Only sharing with other people, by pushing and pulling, needs a network.
why_wrong: Anything stored on GitHub lives on a website, and reaching it needs a connection; what Arjun is using is the copy on his own disk.
Git is distributed rather than centralized, and a centralized system would refuse his commits outright while he was offline.
Git does not queue commits for later; they are written into the local repository immediately and permanently.

questions.q: Git was created by:
options: Linus Torvalds, in 2005, for the development of the Linux kernel
the GitHub company, which later released it to the public
Dennis Ritchie, together with the C programming language
the Apache Software Foundation, as a successor to Subversion
questions.explain: Git came out of the Linux kernel project: Linus Torvalds, who had started Linux, wrote Git in 2005 because the kernel team needed a fast distributed system of its own. It is free and open source, which is one reason it spread far beyond Linux.
why_wrong: GitHub is a hosting website built on top of Git and it came later; it did not create Git.
Dennis Ritchie is associated with C and Unix, decades before Git existed.
Apache is associated with Subversion, a centralized system that Git competes with rather than descends from.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between Git and GitHub?
options: Git is the version control software installed on your computer; GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories online
GitHub is the version control software, and Git is the website that stores the repositories
Git and GitHub are two names for exactly the same product
Git is the paid commercial edition of the free GitHub tool
questions.explain: Git is a program that runs on your own machine and does the actual version control work. GitHub is one of several websites, along with GitLab and Bitbucket, that host Git repositories so they can be shared. You can use Git for years without ever creating a GitHub account.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: the software you install is Git, and the hosting website is GitHub.
They are different things altogether - one is a tool you install, the other is a service you visit.
Git is free and open source, and GitHub is a separate hosting service, not a paid edition of the same tool.

questions.q: Kavya spots a spelling mistake in a public project on GitHub, but she is not a collaborator and has no write access to it. What is the normal way for her to offer the correction?
options: Fork the repository to her own account, commit the fix in her copy, then open a pull request asking the owner to merge it
Clone the repository to her laptop, commit the fix there, and push it straight to the original project
Open an issue describing the mistake, since an issue is the only way to change a repository you do not own
Star the repository, because starring gives a user write access to the project
questions.explain: A fork is your own copy of somebody else's repository under your GitHub account, and in your own copy you do have write access. You commit the fix there and then open a pull request, which proposes the change so the original owner can review it and merge it. Cloning is different: it copies the repository to your computer and gives you no rights over the original.
why_wrong: Cloning gives her the files on her laptop, but the push would be rejected because she has no write access to the original repository.
Opening an issue is a fair way to report the mistake, but it only describes the problem instead of offering the corrected text, and it is certainly not the only route.
Starring merely bookmarks a project so she can find it again; it grants no permissions at all.

questions.q: Immediately after installing Git, which command is normally used to confirm that the installation worked?
options: git --version
git install
git init
git status
questions.explain: git --version simply asks Git to print the version it is running. If a version number appears, Git is installed and reachable from your terminal; if the shell replies that the command was not found, the installation or the system path is the problem. It is the usual first check, before you configure your name and email.
why_wrong: There is no git install command - installing is done by the installer you download from git-scm.com, not by Git itself.
git init starts a brand new repository in the current folder and leaves a .git directory behind, so it changes your folder instead of reporting on the installation.
git status reports on files inside an existing repository, so it has nothing useful to say straight after installation.

questions.q: Rohit makes his first few commits and notices that the history shows an unfamiliar default name as the author instead of his own. Which command sets this correctly for every repository on his user account?
options: git config --global user.name "Rohit Sharma"
git config --local user.name "Rohit Sharma"
git config --list
git --version
questions.explain: Every commit stores an author name, and Git takes that name from your configuration. Setting user.name with --global writes it once for your user account, so it applies in every repository you work in from then on. Commits already made keep the old name; the new setting affects commits made afterwards.
why_wrong: The --local form stores the name in one repository only, so he would have to repeat it in every project he starts.
This only displays the settings that already exist; it changes nothing.
This prints the installed version of Git and has nothing to do with the author recorded on a commit.

questions.q: Why does Git expect you to set user.name and user.email before you begin working?
options: because every commit records who made it, so Git needs an identity to attach to each one
because Git uses those two values to create a GitHub account for you
because Git verifies the email address with a server before it will accept the first commit
because the email address acts as the password that unlocks the repository
questions.explain: A commit is a snapshot plus its metadata: a message, a date and an author. The name and email you configure are what Git writes into that author field, which is how the history can later answer the question of who changed a given line. Git never checks the address and never sends mail to it; it simply records it.
why_wrong: Accounts are created by you on the GitHub website; Git's configuration has no connection to that.
Git contacts no server to check the address - it records whatever you type, which is why commits work offline.
There is no password involved: the email is a label written onto your commits, not a key to the repository.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes git fetch from git pull?
options: git fetch downloads the remote's new commits without merging them, while git pull downloads them and merges them into your current branch
git fetch downloads the remote's new commits and merges them, while git pull only reports that new commits exist
Both download and merge the remote's commits; the difference is that git pull also uploads your own commits
git fetch copies a whole repository to your computer for the first time, while git pull creates a new branch from it
questions.explain: git fetch brings the remote's new commits into your local repository but leaves your own branch untouched, so you can look at what has arrived before combining it with your work. git pull does that same download and then merges the new commits into the branch you are on. A short way to remember it is that pull equals fetch plus merge.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: merging is what git pull adds, and git fetch deliberately stops short of changing your branch.
Neither command uploads anything - sending your own commits to the remote is the job of git push.
Copying a repository for the first time is git clone, and neither fetch nor pull creates a branch for you.

questions.q: Sana commits her personal projects with her personal email address, but one college repository must carry her university address instead. What should she do?
options: Inside that repository, run git config user.email with the university address, because a local setting overrides the global one there
Run git config --global user.email with the university address, since that is the only place an email can be set
Run git config --system user.email with the university address so that the machine handles it
Delete the global setting, so that Git asks her which address to use at each commit
questions.explain: Git reads configuration at three levels - system, global and local - and the most specific level wins. Setting user.email inside a single repository sets it at the local level, which is the default when you leave the flag out inside a repo, so only that project's commits carry the university address while everything else keeps the global personal one.
why_wrong: A --global value applies to every repository belonging to her user account, so this would put the university address on her personal projects too.
The --system level applies to every user on the computer, which is broader still than global and again not per-repository.
Git never prompts for an address at commit time; with nothing configured it either stops with an error or guesses one from the system.

questions.q: You run one command inside an ordinary project folder, and Git creates a hidden .git directory that turns the folder into a repository. Which command did you run?
options: git init
git clone <url>
git status
git add .
questions.explain: git init is what turns a plain folder into a Git repository. It creates the hidden .git directory, which is where every commit and all the history will be stored from then on. Until that folder exists, no other Git command has anywhere to record anything.
why_wrong: git clone <url> downloads an existing repository together with its full history from a remote; it does not start a brand new empty repository from your own folder.
git status only reports what is untracked, modified or staged inside a repository that already exists.
git add . stages changes in a folder that is already a repository; it cannot create the .git directory.

questions.q: A change passes through Git's three areas before it is stored permanently. What is the correct order?
options: Staging area -> Working directory -> Repository
Working directory -> Staging area -> Repository
Repository -> Working directory -> Staging area
Working directory -> Repository -> Staging area
questions.explain: You edit files in the working directory, then mark the changes you want with git add, which puts them in the staging area (also called the index), and finally git commit stores that selected snapshot in the repository. The staging area exists so you can choose exactly what goes into a commit instead of committing everything you happen to have touched.
why_wrong: Nothing can be staged before it has been edited, so the working directory must come first.
The repository is the end of the journey, not the start; commits arrive there last.
Changes are staged before they are committed, so the repository comes last rather than in the middle.

questions.q: Which command marks a changed file as ready to be included in the next commit, placing it in the staging area (also called the index)?
options: git status
git commit -m "msg"
git add notes.txt
git push
questions.explain: git add moves a change from the working directory into the staging area, which is Git's waiting room for the next commit. git add notes.txt stages one file, while git add . stages everything that changed in the folder. Nothing is permanent yet at this point; staging only decides what the next commit will contain.
why_wrong: git status reports the current state of your files but changes nothing, so it cannot move anything into the staging area.
git commit -m records what is ALREADY staged into the repository; it is the step after staging, not the staging step itself.
git push uploads commits that already exist in your local repository to the remote.

questions.q: What exactly does git commit -m "Fix login bug" record?
options: Every file currently in the working directory, whether or not it was staged
Only the changes that were staged, stored as a snapshot carrying that message
The changes, and it immediately uploads them to GitHub
A note on the project's GitHub Issues page describing the fix
questions.explain: A commit is a permanent snapshot of what is in the staging area, saved with an author, a date, a message and a unique identifier (a SHA hash). Anything you changed but never staged with git add is simply left out of that snapshot. The message after -m is what lets you (and everyone else) understand later why the change was made.
why_wrong: Changes that were never staged with git add are left out; Git commits what is in the staging area.
Committing is entirely local; sending commits to GitHub is a separate step done with git push.
Issues are a GitHub web feature for tracking bugs and tasks; they have nothing to do with a commit's -m message.

questions.q: You want a compact list of the project's past commits, one line each. Which command gives you that?
options: git log --oneline
git diff
git status
git branch
questions.explain: git log prints the commit history with the newest commit first, showing each commit's identifier, author, date and message. Adding --oneline squeezes each commit onto a single line, which is far easier to scan when the project has many commits. It reads history only; it changes nothing in your files.
why_wrong: git diff shows the actual line-by-line changes you have made, not the list of past commits.
git status describes the state of your files right now and shows no history at all.
git branch lists the branches in the repository, not the commits on them.

questions.q: Run on its own with no extra arguments, what does git diff show?
options: The differences between two branches only
The changes in your working directory that have not yet been staged
The list of all commits with their messages
The files that are being ignored because of .gitignore
questions.explain: git diff answers the question "what have I changed but not yet marked for commit?" It prints the line-by-line difference between the files in your working directory and what is currently staged. It is the natural command to run just before git add, so you can see exactly what you are about to stage.
why_wrong: Comparing branches is possible with extra arguments, but git diff on its own reports your own uncommitted, unstaged work.
Listing commits with their messages is the job of git log.
Ignored files are listed in .gitignore; git diff does not report them.

questions.q: In the command git remote add origin https://github.com/user/project.git, what is "origin"?
options: The name of the branch that will be created
The GitHub username of the repository owner
The conventional short name given to that remote repository's URL
The message attached to the first commit
questions.explain: A remote is just a nickname for a URL that your local repository can push to and pull from, and origin is the name everyone conventionally uses for the main remote. Typing git push origin main is far easier than retyping the whole https:// URL each time. The name is only a convention, but sticking to it keeps commands readable for everyone.
why_wrong: Branch names such as main or master are separate from remote names, and this command creates no branch.
The username does appear inside the URL, but origin is a label you attach to the remote itself.
Commit messages are supplied with git commit -m and have nothing to do with adding a remote.

questions.q: Which file lists the files and folders Git should never track, such as build output, node_modules and files containing secrets?
options: README.md
.gitignore
.git
index.html
questions.explain: A .gitignore file sits in the repository and names patterns Git should skip, so those files never get staged or committed by accident. It keeps the history clean of things nobody needs to share, and it is the standard protection against committing passwords and API keys. Files listed there simply stop appearing as untracked in git status.
why_wrong: README.md describes the project and is what visitors see on the repository's front page.
.git is the hidden folder where Git stores the repository itself, including every commit; it is not a list of exclusions.
index.html is an ordinary project file with no special meaning to Git.

questions.q: You are currently on the main branch and you run git merge feature. What does Git do?
options: Brings the commits from feature into main
Brings the commits from main into feature
Switches you over to the feature branch
Uploads the feature branch to GitHub
questions.explain: git merge always pulls the named branch INTO the branch you are standing on. So on main, git merge feature adds the feature work to main and leaves feature itself untouched. Checking which branch you are on before merging is the habit that prevents merging in the wrong direction.
why_wrong: That is the opposite direction; to do that you would first switch to feature and then run git merge main.
Switching branches is done with git checkout <branch> or the newer git switch <branch>.
Uploading a branch to the remote is git push, not git merge.

questions.q: You have just installed Git, and before your first commit you want to set the author name Git will record in every repository you work on under your user account. Which command does that?
options: git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --local user.name "Your Name"
git commit -m "Your Name"
git init "Your Name"
questions.explain: Every commit stores an author, so Git asks you to identify yourself once after installation with git config --global user.name and git config --global user.email. The --global flag stores the setting for your user account, so it applies to every repository on the machine instead of just one. You can check what is set with git config --list.
why_wrong: git config --local sets the value for the current repository only, so it would not apply to the other repositories you work on.
git commit -m supplies a message describing a change; it does not store your identity as a setting.
git init creates a new repository in the current folder and takes no name setting like this.

questions.q: Which GitHub feature is used to track bugs and tasks for a project?
options: Stars
Issues
Forks
Pull requests
questions.explain: Issues are GitHub's built-in tracker: each one is a numbered entry describing a bug to fix or a task to do, and people discuss it in the comments until it is closed. They live with the repository, so the plan and the code stay in one place. Many projects also link a pull request to the issue it fixes.
why_wrong: Stars simply bookmark a project and signal that you like it.
A fork is your own copy of somebody else's repository under your account.
A pull request proposes a set of changes so the owner can review and merge them.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a centralized version control system such as Subversion and a distributed one such as Git?
options: In a centralized system the full history lives on one central server, while in a distributed system every developer's clone holds the full history
In a centralized system every developer holds the full history, while in a distributed system it exists only on a server
A centralized system can store only text files, while a distributed system can store files of any type
A centralized system keeps no commit history at all; only a distributed system records commits
questions.explain: In a centralized VCS the single repository and all of its history sit on one server, so you need a network connection to commit and that server is a single point of failure. In a distributed VCS such as Git, cloning copies the entire repository including its complete history, so you can commit, branch and read the log offline. It also means every clone acts as a backup, and developers sync with each other by pushing and pulling.
why_wrong: That reverses the two; holding a complete copy of the history on each developer's machine is exactly what makes Git distributed.
Both kinds happily store any type of file; the difference is where the history is kept, not what may be stored.
Centralized systems such as Subversion record commits and keep full history too, but that history lives only on the central server.

questions.q: Priya has edited several files in her project and also created two new ones. Before committing, she wants one summary telling her which files are new, which are changed, and which are already staged. Which command gives her that?
options: git log
git status
git commit -m "check"
git branch
questions.explain: git status is the command you run constantly while working, because it reports exactly where every file stands right now: untracked, modified but unstaged, or staged for the next commit. It also usually hints at the command to run next. It is read-only, so running it can never break anything.
why_wrong: git log lists commits that were already made and says nothing about the files she has just edited.
Committing would record her work rather than describe it, and it would only capture what is already staged.
git branch lists branches, not file changes.

questions.q: Rahul cloned his team's repository, edited some files, and ran git add . and git commit -m "Add contact page" without errors. But when he refreshes the project page on GitHub, his change is nowhere to be seen. What does he still need to do?
options: git push
git pull
Run git init in the folder again
Run git add . again
questions.explain: Committing stores a snapshot in the repository on his own laptop; Git is distributed, so nothing leaves the machine until you say so. git push is the step that uploads his local commits to the remote, which is when GitHub finally shows them. This local-then-push split is why you can commit happily with no internet.
why_wrong: git pull brings other people's commits down from the remote; it does not send his up.
git init would try to start a new repository, but his repository already exists from the clone.
git add . stages changes, and his changes are already committed; staging again sends nothing to GitHub.

questions.q: Aman shares a GitHub repository with three classmates. Before he starts today's work, he wants the commits they pushed yesterday brought down and merged into his branch so he is not editing an out-of-date copy. What should he run first?
options: git push
git pull
git log
git status
questions.explain: git pull downloads the new commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch in one step, which is why it is the standard way to begin a session on a shared project. Starting from the latest code means fewer and smaller conflicts later. The habit is simple: pull before you start, push when you finish.
why_wrong: git push sends his own commits up and brings nothing down.
git log only shows the history he already has on his own machine.
git status describes his own files and never contacts the remote.

questions.q: Sana wants to see what her teammates have pushed to the remote, but she is halfway through a delicate change and does not want anything merged into her working files yet. Which command fits?
options: git pull
git fetch
git checkout main
git diff
questions.explain: git fetch downloads the remote's new commits into your repository but leaves your branch and your working files exactly as they are, so you can inspect what arrived before deciding anything. git pull is really fetch plus an automatic merge, which is the part she wants to postpone. When she is ready, she can merge the fetched work herself.
why_wrong: git pull would download the new commits AND merge them into her branch, which is precisely what she wants to avoid right now.
Switching branches only moves her around history she already has; it downloads nothing.
git diff compares her own local changes and never contacts the remote.

questions.q: Kiran wants to attempt a risky redesign of his site's homepage, but the current version must stay safe and working so he can go back to it at any time. What is the proper Git way to do this?
options: Copy the whole folder to homepage_backup before editing anything
Create a new branch, switch to it, and do the experiment there
Edit the files and simply avoid committing until he is sure it works
Delete the .git folder and start a fresh repository for the experiment
questions.explain: A branch is an independent line of development, so commits made on it do not touch main at all. He can experiment freely, and if it fails he just switches back to main, which is untouched; if it works, he merges the branch in. This is exactly what branching exists for, and it costs almost nothing to create one.
why_wrong: Copying folders by hand is the habit version control was invented to replace; the copy carries no history and drifts out of date.
Leaving everything uncommitted means there is no safe point to return to, and a single bad save can destroy the working version.
Deleting .git throws away the whole history of the project, which is the opposite of keeping the working version safe.

questions.q: Meera merges a teammate's branch into her own. Git stops partway and reports a conflict in one file, because both of them changed the same lines. What has happened, and what should she do?
options: The repository is corrupted, so she should delete it and clone again
Git cannot decide automatically which version to keep, so she edits the file to resolve it and then commits the resolution
Git has thrown away both versions, so she must retype the file from memory
The remote is unreachable, so she should run git push to reconnect
questions.explain: A merge conflict simply means two branches changed the same lines and Git refuses to guess which one is right. Git marks both versions inside the file and hands the decision to you; you edit the file into the version you actually want, stage it, and commit. Conflicts are a routine part of teamwork, not a sign that anything is broken.
why_wrong: A conflict is normal and expected; the repository is perfectly healthy, and re-cloning would just throw away her work.
Git keeps both versions and marks them inside the file so she can choose; nothing has been discarded.
Conflicts are decided locally between two sets of commits; the network is not involved.

questions.q: Dev has a finished folder of project files on his laptop that has never been under version control, and an empty repository waiting on GitHub. Which sequence gets his work onto it?
options: git init -> git add . -> git commit -m "first commit" -> git remote add origin <url> -> git push -u origin main
git clone <url> -> git add . -> git commit -m "first commit" -> git push
git add . -> git init -> git push -> git commit -m "first commit"
git remote add origin <url> -> git push -> git init -> git commit -m "first commit"
questions.explain: For a brand-new project the order follows the three areas: create the repository, stage the files, commit them locally, then connect a remote and push. git init must come first because every later command needs the .git folder to exist, and the remote can only be added to a repository that already exists. The -u on the first push also remembers the remote and branch, so later you can just type git push.
why_wrong: git clone is for a repository that already has content, but his GitHub repository is empty and his files are already on his laptop.
Nothing can be staged before git init has created the repository, and pushing before committing would send nothing.
A remote cannot be added before git init has created the repository, and there is no commit yet to push.

questions.q: Nisha spots a bug in a stranger's public project on GitHub and has written a fix. She has no write access to that repository. What is the normal way to offer her fix?
options: Clone the repository, fix the bug, and push straight to the owner's repository
Fork the repository to her own account, commit the fix there, and open a pull request
Add herself as a collaborator on the owner's repository and then push the fix
Download the files as a ZIP, fix them, and attach the ZIP as a comment
questions.explain: Forking gives her a copy of the project under her own GitHub account, where she has full write access to commit the fix. A pull request then proposes those commits back to the original repository so the owner can review the exact changes and merge them if they agree. This fork-then-pull-request flow is how open source contribution works for people who are not collaborators.
why_wrong: Cloning only copies the project to her computer, and pushing back to someone else's repository requires write access she does not have, so the push is rejected.
Only the repository's owner can grant collaborator access; you cannot add yourself.
Uploading a ZIP of edited files is not how changes are reviewed on GitHub, whereas a pull request shows the exact line-by-line changes.

questions.q: What does the term malware refer to?
options: Any software written deliberately to damage, disrupt, steal from or gain unauthorised access to a computer or network
Any software that runs slowly and uses more memory than it should
Any software that is distributed free of charge over the internet
Any software that has not been updated to its latest version
questions.explain: Malware is simply short for malicious software. What makes a program malware is the intention behind it - it is written to damage, disrupt, spy on or break into a system without permission. Price, size or age have nothing to do with it.
why_wrong: Poor performance is a symptom of many ordinary problems, including badly written but harmless software, so slowness by itself proves nothing about intent.
Being free is a matter of licensing and price; enormous amounts of free software are perfectly safe.
An out-of-date program may carry unpatched security weaknesses, but missing an update is not the same as being written to cause harm.

questions.q: Which characteristic best describes a computer virus?
options: It attaches itself to a host program or file and spreads only when a user runs or opens that file
It travels across a network on its own with no human involvement at all
It encrypts the victim's documents and demands a payment for the key
It hides its own presence while giving an attacker administrator rights
questions.explain: A virus cannot live on its own - it rides inside a legitimate program or file, and it stays dormant until a person runs or opens that host. Those two marks, needing a host and needing user action, are exactly what separate a virus from a worm in every exam question on this topic.
why_wrong: Spreading by itself with no human action is the defining behaviour of a worm, not a virus.
Encryption plus a payment demand is ransomware.
Hidden administrator-level control is the description of a rootkit.

questions.q: Rohit copies a game setup file from a friend's pen drive and nothing happens for several days. The moment he finally runs the setup, other programs on his laptop start failing and the same infection turns up in files he shares afterwards. Machines he never gave a copy to stay clean. Which type of malware is this?
options: Worm
Virus
Botnet
Adware
questions.explain: Two details settle it: the infection waited until Rohit ran the file, and it spread only to files and people that received a copy. That is a virus - it needs a host file and a human action, and it reproduces by infecting other files rather than by crossing the network on its own.
why_wrong: A worm would not have waited for Rohit to run anything, and it would have reached other machines on the network by itself.
A botnet is a large group of machines under one remote controller used for attacks; here nobody is controlling Rohit's laptop from outside.
Adware's signature is unwanted advertisements and browser changes, not infected files and programs that stop working.

questions.q: What makes a worm different from the other malware types in the way it spreads?
options: It requires the user to open an infected attachment every single time it spreads
It is a standalone program that copies itself and spreads across networks with no host program and no user action
It must be installed by a user who believes it is a useful application
It can only travel through pen drives and other removable media
questions.explain: A worm is self-contained and self-propelling: it does not attach to a host file and it does not wait for anyone to click. Because it multiplies unchecked it eats bandwidth, memory and disk space, which is why a worm outbreak shows up as a slow or crashing network.
why_wrong: Needing the user to act each time is the virus's limitation; the worm's whole point is that it does not need it.
Being installed voluntarily by a deceived user describes a trojan horse.
Worms typically exploit network weaknesses or mail themselves to contacts; removable media is not what defines them.

questions.q: An hour after one student opened an e-mail attachment, every machine in the computer lab has slowed to a crawl and the network is flooded with traffic. Nobody else opened anything, yet the same program is now running on all the machines. Which type of malware is this?
options: Trojan horse
Rootkit
Worm
Spyware
questions.explain: The infection reached machines whose users did nothing, and it saturated the network as it multiplied. Self-spreading across a network plus heavy consumption of bandwidth and memory is the classic worm picture.
why_wrong: A trojan does not copy itself anywhere; it stays on the machine where the deceived user installed it.
A rootkit works to stay hidden and hold quiet administrator control, not to announce itself by flooding a network.
Spyware depends on going unnoticed, so choking the network with traffic would defeat its own purpose.

questions.q: Which statement about a Trojan horse is correct?
options: It disguises itself as something useful or desirable so the user installs it, and it does not replicate itself
It automatically copies itself to every drive and machine it can reach
It is a network of infected computers operated by a remote controller
Its main effect is to display advertisements in the user's browser
questions.explain: A trojan gets in through deception rather than through any technical self-spreading ability - a free game, a cracked application, a fake updater. Once installed it may open a backdoor, steal data or pull down more malware, but the user has to be tricked into running it each time, because it never copies itself.
why_wrong: Automatic self-copying is what viruses and worms do; a trojan's spread depends entirely on fresh victims being deceived.
A network of remotely controlled infected machines is a botnet.
Unwanted advertising is the mark of adware.

questions.q: Neha installs a cracked copy of a paid video editor from a random website. The editor actually works, but a week later the IT team tells her someone has been connecting to her laptop remotely. The program never copied itself anywhere else. Which type of malware is this?
options: Worm
Virus
Trojan horse
Ransomware
questions.explain: Neha installed it herself because it looked like the software she wanted, and it then quietly opened a backdoor for remote access. Disguise plus consent obtained by deception, with no self-replication at all, is the definition of a trojan horse.
why_wrong: A worm spreads itself to other machines over the network; this program stayed exactly where it was installed.
A virus reproduces by infecting other files and programs, and nothing here reproduced.
Ransomware announces itself by locking or encrypting files and demanding money; Neha's files were never touched.

questions.q: A program that secretly records every key a user types in order to capture passwords is an example of which type of malware?
options: Adware
Spyware
Worm
Rootkit
questions.explain: A keylogger is a form of spyware: it installs quietly and monitors the user, sending what it captures to a third party without consent. Spyware is classified by what it does - secret surveillance and data theft - not by how it arrived on the machine.
why_wrong: Adware exists to push advertisements at the user and is visible by design, not secret.
A worm is defined by self-replication across networks, not by recording what a user types.
A rootkit is about concealment and administrator-level control, not about capturing keystrokes.

questions.q: Aman's laptop behaves completely normally, but over two weeks his e-mail, college portal and bank account are all accessed by someone else. His antivirus eventually finds a program that had been running quietly since he installed a free screen-recording tool, sending information about his activity to an unknown server. Which type of malware is this?
options: Ransomware
Adware
Spyware
Worm
questions.explain: Nothing was destroyed, nothing was demanded and nothing was displayed - the machine simply leaked Aman's information to somebody else for two weeks. Silent monitoring and theft of credentials is precisely what spyware does, and staying unnoticed is what makes it effective.
why_wrong: Ransomware makes itself obvious at once by locking files and demanding payment; it has no reason to sit quietly for weeks.
Adware would have filled his screen with advertisements instead of leaving the laptop behaving normally.
A worm's multiplication would have hit other machines and eaten bandwidth rather than silently harvesting his logins.

questions.q: What does ransomware do to its victim?
options: Encrypts the victim's files or locks the whole system and demands a payment in exchange for the decryption key
Quietly forwards the victim's browsing history to advertising companies
Turns the machine into a remotely controlled zombie used for attacks on other targets
Attaches itself to other programs so that it spreads whenever they are run
questions.explain: Ransomware combines two things: encryption and extortion. The files stay on the disk but become unreadable without a key the attacker holds, and a demand for payment, usually in cryptocurrency and often with a countdown, appears on screen. Paying does not guarantee recovery, which is why tested offline backups are the real defence.
why_wrong: Quietly harvesting browsing data describes spyware and tracking adware; ransomware wants to be seen.
Being remotely controlled as one machine among thousands describes a botnet.
Attaching to other programs to spread when they run describes a virus.

questions.q: Priya's project folder now contains files named report.docx.locked and presentation.pptx.locked, and a full-screen message demands payment in cryptocurrency within 48 hours in exchange for a key. Which type of malware has hit her machine?
options: Ransomware
Spyware
Rootkit
Trojan horse
questions.explain: Her files are still there but unreadable, and a payment is being demanded for the key - encryption plus extortion, which is ransomware exactly. Priya should not pay; the dependable way out is a clean offline backup, which is why backups matter before an attack, not after.
why_wrong: Spyware's entire method is to stay unnoticed while stealing information, so it would never put a payment demand on the screen.
A rootkit works to hide itself and keep quiet administrator control; a full-screen ransom note is the opposite of hiding.
A trojan horse describes a disguise used to get malware installed; the encryption-and-extortion behaviour on screen is what names this one.

questions.q: Which description fits adware best?
options: Software that automatically displays or downloads unwanted advertisements, often arriving bundled with free software the user installed
Software that encrypts a user's documents until a fee is paid
Software that gives an attacker hidden administrator control of a machine
Software that copies itself across a network and consumes its bandwidth
questions.explain: Adware is defined by the unwanted advertising it forces on the user - pop-ups, injected banners, redirects, a changed home page - and it usually rides in with free downloads. It often tracks browsing to target those ads, so it is mainly a nuisance and a privacy problem rather than a destroyer of data.
why_wrong: Encrypting documents until a fee is paid is ransomware.
Hidden administrator control is a rootkit.
Copying itself across a network and eating bandwidth is a worm.

questions.q: After installing a free PDF converter, Kiran finds that his browser home page has been changed, pop-up advertisements appear on pages that never had them, and some searches get redirected elsewhere. His files are all intact and nothing is being demanded of him. Which type of malware is this?
options: Ransomware
Adware
Worm
Rootkit
questions.explain: Bundled with a free download, and its whole visible effect is advertising and browser interference - that is adware. It is irritating and bad for privacy because it usually tracks browsing to target the ads, but it is not destroying his data.
why_wrong: Ransomware would have encrypted or locked his files and demanded payment; his files are untouched.
A worm would show up as infections on other machines and network congestion, not as advertisements in his browser.
A rootkit's aim is to remain invisible, and changing the home page while throwing up pop-ups is the loudest behaviour possible.

questions.q: Why are rootkits considered especially difficult to detect and remove?
options: They give an attacker administrator-level control while actively hiding themselves and other malware from the user and from security software
They spread across networks faster than any other kind of malware
They are the only malware capable of encrypting files
They are automatically bundled with every free download from the internet
questions.explain: A rootkit buries itself deep in the operating system, so it both holds root or administrator privileges and conceals its own presence, along with anything else the attacker has planted. Because the very tools you would use to look for it can be fooled, a full reinstall of the operating system is often the only trustworthy cure.
why_wrong: Speed of network spread is the worm's trait; a rootkit is about privilege and concealment, not racing across a network.
Ransomware is the type defined by encryption for extortion, and encryption is not what characterises a rootkit.
Arriving bundled with free software is typical of adware, and in any case no malware comes with every download.

questions.q: An attacker has administrator control of a college server. The security software reports the system as clean, some system tools list fewer running processes than the administrator knows are there, and the technicians conclude that reinstalling the operating system is the only reliable fix. Which type of malware best explains this?
options: Adware
Rootkit
Ransomware
Virus
questions.explain: Three clues point one way: administrator-level control, active concealment that makes the security tools report a clean system, and a reinstall being the only dependable cure. That combination of privilege plus stealth is what a rootkit is.
why_wrong: Adware is a visible nuisance that shows advertisements; it neither grants administrator control nor hides from security software.
Ransomware makes its presence unmistakable with a ransom demand, and nothing is being demanded here.
A virus infects host files and is normally found and cleaned by antivirus software rather than being invisible to it.

questions.q: In a botnet, what is the role of the infected computers?
options: Each infected machine, called a bot or zombie, is controlled remotely by the attacker and used together with the others for attacks such as DDoS or mass spam
Each infected machine encrypts its own files and waits for its owner to pay
Each infected machine earns money for the attacker purely by showing advertisements to its owner
Each infected machine protects the attacker by deleting all of its own log files
questions.explain: A botnet's power comes from numbers: thousands of ordinary machines, each quietly infected, all obeying one attacker through a command-and-control server. The owners usually have no idea, and the combined capacity gets used to flood a target with traffic in a DDoS attack, send spam, commit click fraud or mine cryptocurrency.
why_wrong: Encrypting files and waiting for payment is ransomware acting on one victim, not machines being pooled for attacks.
Showing advertisements is adware's business model, and it involves no remote controller directing the machine.
Log deletion may be part of an attacker's cover-up, but it is not what turns a machine into a bot.

questions.q: Sameer's laptop seems perfectly fine, but his internet provider writes to say the laptop has been sending huge volumes of traffic to one particular website every night, together with thousands of other machines, as part of an attack on that site. What has most likely happened to his laptop?
options: It has been hit by ransomware
It has been infected with spyware
It has been recruited into a botnet
It has picked up adware
questions.explain: Sameer's machine is not the target here - it is the weapon. Being one of thousands of remotely controlled machines aimed at flooding a single site with traffic is exactly a botnet carrying out a DDoS attack, and the giveaway is that the owner notices nothing.
why_wrong: Ransomware would have locked or encrypted Sameer's own files and demanded money from him; his laptop works normally.
Spyware steals information from the victim, whereas here the laptop is being used to attack someone else's website.
Adware's payoff is advertisements shown to Sameer, not traffic directed at a third party in the middle of the night.

questions.q: Which habit gives the best protection against picking up malware while installing new software?
options: Downloading it only from the software maker's official website or an official app store
Downloading whichever copy appears first in the search results, since search engines rank the safest sites highest
Switching the antivirus off during the installation so that it does not interrupt
Preferring a cracked copy from a file-sharing site so that no account details have to be given
questions.explain: Most malware reaches ordinary users through the download itself, so where the file comes from matters more than anything you do afterwards. An official site or store is the one place where the file you receive is the file the maker published; anywhere else the installer may have been repackaged with a trojan inside. Keeping the antivirus switched on with current definitions backs that habit up.
why_wrong: Search rankings are shaped by advertising and by deliberate manipulation, and attackers work hard to push convincing fake download pages to the top.
Turning the antivirus off removes the one check that might catch a malicious installer at the exact moment it runs.
Cracked software is one of the commonest trojan carriers, because the file has already been modified by someone you cannot identify.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes spyware from adware?
options: Spyware secretly collects the user's information and sends it to a third party, while adware's main effect is unwanted advertising
Spyware fills the screen with pop-ups, while adware records every keystroke
Spyware spreads over networks by itself, while adware needs a host program to attach to
Spyware encrypts files for a ransom, while adware hides the attacker's presence
questions.explain: Both often arrive bundled with free downloads, so students mix them up, but their purposes differ. Spyware is about secrecy and theft of information; adware is about pushing advertisements at you, even though it may track your browsing to choose which ones. One steals quietly, the other annoys openly.
why_wrong: This reverses the two: pop-ups are adware's behaviour and keylogging is a form of spyware.
Self-spreading over networks describes a worm and attaching to a host describes a virus; neither statement is about spyware or adware.
Encrypting for ransom is ransomware and hiding the attacker is a rootkit, so neither half of this statement is correct.

questions.q: Which of these is the most reliable protection against losing your data to ransomware?
options: Paying the ransom quickly, before the countdown on screen runs out
Keeping regular offline backups and checking that they actually restore
Renaming important files so that the malware cannot recognise them
Doing all your daily work from an administrator account
questions.explain: If a clean copy of your data exists somewhere the malware cannot reach, the attacker has nothing to sell you - you wipe the machine and restore. Backups only count if they are kept offline and have actually been tested, because an untested backup discovered to be broken during an emergency is no backup at all.
why_wrong: Paying protects nothing: there is no guarantee a working key arrives, and it funds further attacks.
Ransomware encrypts whatever it finds regardless of file names, so renaming achieves nothing.
Working as administrator makes matters worse, since malware inherits those privileges and can reach more of the system.

questions.q: Why is it recommended that everyday work be done from a standard (non-administrator) user account?
options: Because malware that runs in that session inherits only the limited privileges of that account and can therefore do less damage
Because standard accounts cannot be infected by malware at all
Because antivirus software only functions on standard accounts
Because standard accounts encrypt every file on the disk automatically
questions.explain: Malware runs with whatever rights the logged-in user has. From a standard account it cannot install system-wide software, alter protected settings or reach other users' data nearly as easily, so the blast radius of a mistake is much smaller. It does not make you immune - it limits the damage.
why_wrong: A standard account can certainly be infected; it simply limits what the infection can reach.
Antivirus software works on both kinds of account, and installing or updating it usually needs administrator rights.
Standard accounts do not encrypt anything by themselves; disk encryption is a separate feature you turn on.

questions.q: A worm swept through a company's network last month, spreading by itself through a weakness in a server program that had not been updated for two years. The IT team wants to make sure the same thing cannot happen again. Which measure deals with the cause most directly?
options: Installing operating system and application updates promptly, so known weaknesses are closed before a worm can use them
Buying extra bandwidth so the network can absorb the traffic a future outbreak would create
Installing a second antivirus program on every machine so that two run at the same time
Making every employee change their password once a month
questions.explain: Worms spread by exploiting security weaknesses, and a weakness the vendor has already patched is only dangerous on machines that never applied the patch. Prompt updating closes the exact opening this worm used. The other measures may sound sensible, but none of them removes the hole in the server program.
why_wrong: Extra bandwidth only softens a symptom, the congestion, while the worm still spreads and still infects every unpatched machine.
A second antivirus patches nothing, and two products scanning at once tend to conflict with each other rather than catch more.
The worm broke in through a flaw in the server software, not by guessing anyone's password, so new passwords would not have stopped it.

questions.q: Which statement best describes social engineering?
options: Software that secretly records what you type and sends it to an attacker
Manipulating people into revealing confidential information or performing unsafe actions
Exploiting a flaw in a program's code to take control of a computer
Scrambling data so that an attacker who intercepts it cannot read it
questions.explain: Social engineering targets the person, not the machine. The attacker's tool is persuasion - trust, fear, urgency, curiosity - so no firewall or antivirus can block a user who is talked into handing over their own password. That is exactly why people are described as the weakest link in security.
why_wrong: That is spyware, a keylogging kind of malware; it attacks the machine rather than the person's judgement.
That is a technical exploit of a software vulnerability, which is the opposite of attacking the human being.
That describes encryption, a protective measure, not an attack of any kind.

questions.q: Which social-engineering technique is defined as inventing a believable scenario together with a false identity in order to extract information?
options: Baiting
Dumpster diving
Pretexting
Shoulder surfing
questions.explain: Pretexting is built on a story: a false identity plus a plausible reason for needing the information, such as I am from the IT department and we must verify your account. The invented scenario is what makes the victim feel it is normal to answer. Anyone who contacts you claiming to need your details should be verified independently before you say anything.
why_wrong: Baiting tempts the victim with something attractive, such as an infected USB drive or a free download, rather than telling a story.
Dumpster diving means recovering information from discarded papers or devices, with no conversation with the victim at all.
Shoulder surfing is simply watching someone type a PIN or password, and needs no invented identity.

questions.q: Searching through an organisation's discarded papers, printouts and old devices for useful information is called:
options: Tailgating
Quid pro quo
Baiting
Dumpster diving
questions.explain: Sensitive information often leaves an organisation through the bin - printouts, old statements, discarded hard drives. Dumpster diving is the low-tech technique of recovering it, which is why shredding papers and wiping devices matter. It needs no contact with the victim whatsoever.
why_wrong: Tailgating is following an authorised person through a secure door instead of using your own credentials.
Quid pro quo offers the victim something in return, such as fake free tech support, in exchange for access or credentials.
Baiting leaves something tempting, like a labelled USB drive, for the victim to pick up and use.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a social-engineering technique?
options: Shoulder surfing
A worm that spreads by itself from machine to machine through a software flaw
Quid pro quo
Impersonation
questions.explain: Social engineering always works through a human being who is persuaded, watched or followed. A worm needs no persuasion at all: it copies itself across the network by exploiting a software flaw, which makes it malware rather than social engineering. The other three all depend on a person being tricked or observed.
why_wrong: Shoulder surfing is a social-engineering technique: watching a person as they type their PIN or password.
Quid pro quo is social engineering: the attacker offers something, such as fake technical support, in exchange for credentials.
Impersonation is social engineering: posing as a colleague, technician, delivery agent or official to win trust.

questions.q: What mainly distinguishes spear phishing from ordinary phishing?
options: It is aimed at one specific person or organisation and uses real details about them to be convincing
It is sent in bulk to as many addresses as possible
It is delivered only by SMS rather than by email
It is used only against chief executives and other senior figures
questions.explain: Ordinary phishing is a net thrown wide - the same message to thousands of people, hoping a few bite. Spear phishing is a single tailored message that uses real details about you: your name, your course, your manager's name. Because those details are correct, the usual clue of a generic greeting disappears, which makes it much harder to spot.
why_wrong: Bulk sending to as many recipients as possible describes ordinary phishing, not the spear variant.
Phishing delivered by SMS is called smishing; spear phishing can arrive through email, SMS or any other channel.
Targeting only senior, high-value people is whaling, which is one particular kind of spear phishing.

questions.q: A carefully crafted phishing email aimed specifically at a company's CEO or a college's principal is known as:
options: Vishing
Clone phishing
Whaling
Baiting
questions.explain: Whaling is spear phishing pointed at the biggest fish - a director, a CEO, a principal - because that person's approval or account is worth far more to the attacker. Such messages are usually polished and business-like, often about payments, contracts or legal matters. The technique is the same as spear phishing; only the seniority of the target differs.
why_wrong: Vishing is phishing carried out by voice call, which describes the channel used rather than who is targeted.
Clone phishing copies a genuine message you already received and swaps its link or attachment for a malicious one.
Baiting relies on a tempting object such as an infected USB drive or a free download of paid software.

questions.q: Phishing that is carried out by voice call, such as a caller claiming your electricity connection will be cut tonight unless you confirm your details, is called:
options: Smishing
Vishing
Whaling
Pretexting
questions.explain: Vishing is voice phishing: the same fraud that would be smishing over SMS becomes vishing when it arrives as a phone call. A live human voice earns trust far more quickly than text, and the caller manufactures a deadline so that you act before you think. Treat anyone who rings you first as unverified and check through a channel you already trust.
why_wrong: Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS or a messaging app, not by a voice call.
Whaling describes who is being targeted, a senior figure, and says nothing about the use of a phone.
Pretexting is the general technique of inventing a false identity and story; it can be used in a call, an email or in person, so it is not the specific name for phone phishing.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical warning sign that an email is phishing?
options: A greeting such as Dear Customer where the real organisation would use your name
A warning that your account will be blocked within 24 hours unless you act immediately
Hovering over the link shows exactly the address that is displayed, on the organisation's genuine domain
An unexpected .zip attachment that you never asked for
questions.explain: The giveaways of phishing are pressure, sloppiness and mismatch: a generic greeting, a deadline, a look-alike sender or link, an attachment out of nowhere. A link whose hidden destination matches the text shown, on the organisation's real domain, is the opposite of a warning sign - that is what an honest message looks like. Always hover before you click so you can see where a link actually goes.
why_wrong: A greeting such as Dear Customer is a classic sign, because an organisation that really holds your account would normally use your name.
Manufactured urgency of exactly this kind is one of the commonest phishing signs.
An unexpected attachment, especially .zip or .exe, is a standard warning sign because it may install malware.

questions.q: Walking to class you find a USB drive lying in the corridor, neatly labelled Placement List 2026 - Final. You are tempted to plug it into a lab computer to see what is on it. Which technique is the attacker most likely using?
options: Tailgating
Vishing
Dumpster diving
Baiting
questions.explain: Leaving infected media where a curious person will find it is baiting: the attacker relies on your curiosity, because you plug the drive in yourself and no defence has to be defeated. A label like Placement List is chosen precisely because students cannot resist it. Hand a found drive to lab staff instead of connecting it to any machine.
why_wrong: Tailgating is following an authorised person through a secure door rather than using your own credentials.
Vishing is a fraudulent voice call, and no call is involved here.
Dumpster diving is recovering information from things that have been thrown away, not planting a device for you to find.

questions.q: You swipe your ID card to enter the department lab. A person you do not recognise, carrying two large cartons and swiping no card of his own, is close behind you and asks you to hold the door. Letting him in would be an example of:
options: Shoulder surfing
Tailgating
Baiting
Quid pro quo
questions.explain: Tailgating, also called piggybacking, means getting through a controlled door on somebody else's authorisation. Carrying boxes is a standard trick, because ordinary politeness makes people hold the door open. The safe response is to let the door close and ask him to enter with his own card or through reception.
why_wrong: Shoulder surfing is watching someone type a password or PIN, which is not what is happening at the door.
Baiting depends on a tempting object, such as an abandoned USB drive, being picked up by the victim.
Quid pro quo means the attacker offers something in exchange, such as fake free technical help.

questions.q: Your phone rings during a lecture. The caller knows your name, says he is from your bank's fraud team, and explains that a suspicious transaction is in progress and he needs the OTP just sent to your phone in order to block it. What should you do?
options: Read out the OTP, since the caller is trying to stop the fraud rather than commit it
Refuse to give the OTP, end the call, and ring the number printed on your bank card to check
Send him the OTP by SMS instead, so that nobody sitting nearby overhears it
Give him only the first three digits so that he can verify you without getting the whole code
questions.explain: A one-time password is the last thing standing between an attacker and your account, and no genuine bank employee ever needs it, because the bank is the side that generated it. Knowing your name proves nothing, since that is easy to obtain. Hang up and call the number printed on your card or shown inside the bank's own app, never a number or a caller that reached you first.
why_wrong: Anyone asking you to read out an OTP is trying to complete a transaction of their own; a real bank never needs the code it has just sent you.
The danger is the attacker receiving the code at all, so changing the channel from speech to text removes nothing.
Partial codes still help an attacker narrow the possibilities, and the correct response is to share none of it.

questions.q: Last week your department genuinely emailed you a PDF of the exam timetable. Today a message that looks identical arrives from a very similar address, with the same subject and wording, except that the attachment has been replaced by a link to download the updated timetable. This is best described as:
options: Clone phishing
Whaling
Quid pro quo
Baiting
questions.explain: Clone phishing takes a real message you already trust, copies it almost exactly, and substitutes a malicious link or attachment. Because you genuinely received the original, the copy feels expected and your guard drops. The tells here are the slightly different sender address and the fact that an attachment has quietly become a link.
why_wrong: Whaling is phishing aimed at a senior, high-value target such as a principal or a CEO, not at an ordinary student.
Quid pro quo involves the attacker offering a service or favour in exchange for access or credentials.
Baiting relies on planting something tempting, typically a physical device or a free download, rather than copying a genuine message.

questions.q: A hostel friend clicked a link in a scholarship verification email, typed his college email address and password into the page that opened, and only then noticed the strange domain in the address bar. He uses that same password on three other accounts. What should he do first?
options: Delete the email, clear the browser history and carry on as normal
Reply to the email asking the sender to delete the details he typed
Change that password everywhere he reused it and turn on multi-factor authentication
Wait a few days and act only if he notices something suspicious on his accounts
questions.explain: Once a password has been typed into an attacker's page, treat it as known to them, and known on every account where it was reused, because attackers try the same pair on other sites within minutes. Changing it everywhere and switching on multi-factor authentication means a stolen password alone is no longer enough to get in. Reporting and deleting the message matters too, but speed on the password is what limits the damage.
why_wrong: Deleting the mail tidies the inbox but leaves a stolen password working on four separate accounts.
Replying confirms that the address is live and reaches the attacker, who has no intention of deleting anything.
Waiting hands the attacker free time; the password was compromised the moment it was typed in.

questions.q: An SMS arrives reading: Dear Customer, your KYC expires today. Update immediately at http://sbi-kyc-verify.link or your account will be frozen. You do hold an account with that bank. This attack is an example of:
options: Whaling
Shoulder surfing
Smishing
Vishing
questions.explain: Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS or a messaging app. Every typical marker is present here: the generic Dear Customer, a same-day deadline, a threat to freeze the account, and a look-alike address that is not the bank's real domain. Do not tap the link - open the bank's own app or type the address you already know.
why_wrong: Whaling describes phishing aimed at a senior figure such as a CEO or principal, not a mass text sent to ordinary customers.
Shoulder surfing means physically watching someone as they type a password or PIN.
Vishing is phishing carried out over a voice call, whereas this attack arrived as a text message.

questions.q: Which factor does the most to make a password hard to crack by a brute force attack?
options: Its length, because each extra character multiplies the number of combinations to try
Replacing o with 0 and a with @ inside a common dictionary word
Adding one exclamation mark to the end of an ordinary word
Changing a short password to a different short password every week
questions.explain: Brute force means trying every possible combination, and the number of combinations grows enormously with each extra character. That is why a long passphrase of several unrelated words beats a short password stuffed with symbols, and why length is the first thing to increase. Mixing character types still helps, but it cannot rescue something that is only six or eight characters long.
why_wrong: Substituting digits for letters is a pattern attackers already build into their cracking lists, so the word is still guessed quickly.
A single symbol appended to a dictionary word is one of the first variations a dictionary attack tries.
Rotating between short passwords keeps the search space small; every one of them is still cracked in the same short time.

questions.q: Which of these is a WEAK password habit?
options: Using a passphrase made of several unrelated words
Using a different password for every account
Using your date of birth so that you never forget it
Changing a password at once when the service reports a breach
questions.explain: Anything about you that other people can find out, such as a birth date, name, phone number or pet's name, is among the first things an attacker tries. Personal details are also easy to harvest from social media, so they make a password predictable rather than secret. A strong password must be unpredictable even to someone who knows you well.
why_wrong: An unrelated-word passphrase is long and unpredictable, which is exactly what makes a password strong and still memorable.
A unique password per account is essential, because one leaked site then cannot unlock the rest of your accounts.
Changing the password immediately after a breach announcement is the correct response, before the leaked value can be reused.

questions.q: Riya used the same password for a shopping site and for her email. Months after the shopping site announced a data leak, someone logs into her email, even though her email provider was never breached. What attack is this?
options: Credential stuffing
Brute force attack
Shoulder surfing
A rootkit infection
questions.explain: Credential stuffing takes username and password pairs leaked from one site and replays them automatically against many other services, betting that people reuse passwords. Riya's email password was never guessed; it was simply handed over by the shopping site's leak. This is the whole reason a password must be unique per account.
why_wrong: Brute force would mean trying every possible combination against her email, which is not what happened here since the password was already known from the leak.
Shoulder surfing means physically watching someone type a password, which does not explain an attack traced back to a site breach.
A rootkit hides an attacker's presence on an infected machine; nothing here suggests her device was infected.

questions.q: An attacker runs a program that tries a long list of common words and previously leaked passwords against one account. This is best described as:
options: A dictionary attack
A brute force attack
Phishing
Social engineering
questions.explain: A dictionary attack works from a prepared word list rather than from every possible combination, which makes it far faster than brute force and very effective against ordinary words. Brute force tries every combination character by character and is defeated mainly by length. Both are automated guessing attacks, but the dictionary version targets the predictability of human choices.
why_wrong: Brute force tries every possible character combination rather than a prepared list, and takes far longer.
Phishing tricks the user into typing the password into a fake page; no guessing program is involved.
Social engineering manipulates a person into revealing the password, which is a human attack rather than an automated one.

questions.q: Arjun has about forty online accounts and admits he reuses one password because he cannot remember more. He wants unique passwords everywhere without forgetting them. What should he do?
options: Keep one very strong password and use it on every account
Use a password manager that generates and stores long unique passwords behind one master password
Save all his passwords in a file named passwords.txt on his desktop
Use one base password and add each site's name to the end of it
questions.explain: A password manager solves exactly this problem: it generates long random passwords, stores them encrypted, and you only have to remember the one master password. That makes uniqueness practical instead of a memory exercise. He should protect the master password well and turn on multi-factor authentication for the manager itself.
